title: Choose your company
hookLine: pick friends who are calm, since moods are catching (On Tranquility 7)

cards: Someone walks into the office in a foul mood, and within twenty minutes three other people are snapping too. Or the opposite: a friend who's simply easy to be around, and shoulders drop the moment they sit down.
Nobody decided either thing. It just spread. Modern psychologists have a name for this: emotional contagion.
Seneca didn't have the name, but he had the observation. In chapter seven of On Tranquility, after work and service, he turns to the people we spend our days with.

teach.h: NOTHING DELIGHTS LIKE A FAITHFUL FRIEND.
teach.b: First, the gift of a friend.
Nothing, Seneca says, delights the mind like a faithful friendship: someone you can tell a secret to as safely as telling yourself, whose talk eases your worry and whose advice helps you decide.
He's not cynical about people. He wants you to have friends. Second, choose with care.
Vices spread by contact, he warns, passing to whoever is closest, the way an illness passes to those who sit by the sick bed.
So pick, as far as you can, people who aren't ruled by their passions: not the rage-prone, not the greedy, not the one always in a panic. Third, don't wait for a saint.
Don't go looking for a perfectly wise friend, Seneca says; people have searched for centuries.
Choose the least bad. Steadiness, not perfection.
Fourth, beware the moaner. The friend he singles out is the one who's always gloomy, who finds a grievance in every piece of news.
Even if they're loyal and kind, a companion who's constantly upset is an enemy to your calm. A fair note: this isn't advice to abandon a friend who's grieving or ill.
Seneca is talking about the mood we keep company with by habit, not the person who needs us right now. And it cuts both ways.
If calm is catching, so are you. Somebody is choosing your company too.

how: People who follow Seneca's advice pay attention to how the company they keep affects their mood, and seek out steady, calm friends.

games.q: choose your company — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca tells his reader to avoid friendship to stay calm
he says nothing delights the mind like a faithful friend.
Seneca says to choose the least bad, not wait for a perfect friend
the perfectly wise are too rare to wait for.
Seneca's advice means abandoning a grieving friend
he means the gloomy mood kept by habit, not a person who needs you.

games.q: you have a loyal, kind friend who complains about everything, every time you meet. what would Seneca say?
o: a constant moaner is an enemy to your calm.
games.why: he names the always-gloomy companion, however loyal, as a threat to tranquility, and tells you to choose company with care.

practice: Bring to mind the five people you spend the most time with, in person or on a screen, and with each face, notice whether your body settles or tightens, without judging them.
Then sit for a moment with the one who settles you most, let some of their steadiness reach you, and ask: when people sit with me, what do they catch?

wordCard.voice: Amicitia. Latin for friendship: Seneca's advice in On Tranquility, since moods and vices spread by contact, so keep close to the steady. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'friendship': which Seneca says delights the mind more than anything.
